# MEASUREMENT audit checklist (v0.15, generated by scripts/skillgen)

62 checks. Each rests on claims from the methods literature, and each one points to where to read more. The 16 sources listed under **Sources** below are the ones cited in the further-reading lines.

**How to read a verdict.** `PASS` / `FLAG` are decided by the stated conditions. `NA` means the check is out of scope for this design — never that the paper was silent. When a check applies and the paper says nothing, the verdict is the one given in *When silent*.

**Evidence scope.** A verdict covers only the text the audit could see. A FLAG on material the paper says is in an appendix or replication package means "not shown here", not "not done" — such flags carry that caveat in the report.

**Thresholds are rules of thumb unless marked otherwise.** Where a cutoff is conventional rather than derived, the item says so, and near-threshold values are reported as borderline rather than silently rounded to a verdict.

## Scope triggers

A check applies only when its scope trigger fires. Triggers key on the paper's own explicit stance and default OUT when the paper is silent.

- **`all`** — Applies to every paper that reports a quantitative measure of anything. No trigger question; never NA.
- **`external_comparison_validation`** — Does the paper state that it supports its measure by comparing it with something outside the measure itself — an official record, a criterion variable, an established alternative instrument, expert judgements, or a benchmark it names? Fires on that stated comparison-as-support. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: reporting a correlation among its own items, or a descriptive correlation the paper does not offer as support for the measure. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`nomological_validation`** — Does the paper state that its measure is supported because it reproduces an expected, known, or theoretically predicted relationship with another variable? Fires on the paper offering that relationship as evidence for the measure. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: reporting a substantive result that happens to match theory, without presenting it as validation of the measure. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`single_item_measure`** — Does the paper state that one question, one indicator, or one coded variable stands for a named concept in its analysis? Fires on the paper's own description of the operationalization (it names the concept and points to a single item). Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a battery whose items are also reported separately, or a single variable that is a direct physical count rather than a stand-in for an abstract concept. Ambiguous cases are NA.
- **`automated_text_measure`** — Does the paper state that a variable was produced from text by a computer procedure — counting words, classifying documents, fitting a topic or scaling model, applying a language model? Fires on the paper's own description of the procedure. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: people reading and coding the text by hand, or text used only as illustration. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`supervised_text_classifier`** — Does the paper state that it hand-labelled a set of documents and used them to train a procedure that then labelled the rest? Fires on that stated training-set-plus-classifier design. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a topic model or other procedure the paper describes as needing no labels, or a dictionary/word-list count. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`unsupervised_text_categories`** — Does the paper state that categories, topics, or clusters were discovered by a model rather than fixed in advance? Fires on the paper naming such a method or describing the categories as estimated from the data. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a classifier trained on a predefined scheme, or an exploratory factor analysis of survey items (not text). Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`dictionary_measure`** — Does the paper state that it scored text by counting words from a list, lexicon, dictionary, or keyword set? Fires on that self-description, whether the list is borrowed or purpose-built. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a trained classifier whose features happen to be words, or a hand-coding scheme that mentions keywords as guidance. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`text_scaling`** — Does the paper state that it placed actors, documents, or units on a latent dimension estimated from text — an ideology score, a position, a one-dimensional scale from word data? Fires on that self-description. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: classifying documents into categories, or scaling roll-call votes or survey items rather than text. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`latent_variable_model`** — Does the paper state that it fitted a measurement model with unobserved variables — factor analysis, structural equation model, item-response model, latent class or latent trait model? Fires on the paper naming such a model. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a principal-components summary the paper does not describe as a latent-variable model, random intercepts used as a nuisance term, or a simple index. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`fitted_measure_downstream`** — Does the paper state that a variable entering a subsequent analysis is the output of a model it fitted — factor scores, latent estimates, classifier predictions, topic proportions, or another model-produced value? Does NOT fire: a directly recorded variable; a simple sum or average of items (that fires sum_or_average_score); a published index used as given without the paper stating it fitted the model. Unclear whether the value came from a fitted model: NA.
- **`alpha_reported`** — Does the paper report a coefficient alpha / Cronbach's alpha figure for a set of items? Fires on the reported number or the paper's statement that alpha was computed. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: reporting inter-coder agreement, omega, composite reliability, or a test-retest correlation. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`sum_or_average_score`** — Does the paper state that the combined variable is a sum, total, count, or unweighted mean of its items? Fires only where the paper names that arithmetic. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a factor score, an item-response score, a weighted index, or a composite whose rule the paper never states (the unstated case is REPORT-08, not this). Ambiguous cases are NA.
- **`established_instrument`** — Does the paper say it used an instrument that already exists — naming it, citing its source publication, or calling it established, standard, validated, or previously used? Near-miss that does NOT fire it: writing items the paper describes as its own, or reusing a variable from a public dataset without naming an instrument. Ambiguous cases are out of scope (NA), never FLAG.
- **`mcmc_estimated`** — Fires when the paper states that its estimates come from a Markov chain Monte Carlo, Gibbs, Hamiltonian, or other posterior sampler. Near-miss: naming a Bayesian prior in a model fitted by optimisation does not fire it. Unclear how the model was fitted: NA.
- **`multi_item_scale`** — Does the paper state that two or more items, indicators, or component sub-measures are combined into one variable it then analyses? Fires on the paper's own description of building a scale, index, factor score, or composite. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: reporting several related variables side by side without combining them, or entering several indicators as separate regressors. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`unsupervised_text`** — Does the paper state that it used a procedure that discovers categories or dimensions from its texts without labels fixed in advance — a topic model, a clustering, an unsupervised scaling? Does NOT fire: a paper stating its categories were fixed in advance and applied by coders or a trained classifier. Unclear: NA.
- **`conjunctive_construct`** — Does the paper state that its concept requires all of its named parts to be present together — that the parts are necessary conditions, defining attributes, or that a case lacking one does not have the concept? Fires only on that explicit statement about the concept's structure (see REPORT-15, which asks any paper combining several components to make the statement). Near-miss that does NOT fire it: listing several dimensions of a concept without saying whether they can substitute for one another. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`standardized_before_aggregation`** — Does the paper state that component variables were standardized, z-scored, normalized, or rescaled to a common range before being combined? Fires on the paper's own description of the rescaling step. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: reporting standardized coefficients in a regression table, or reporting items that happen to share a response scale. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`ordinal_as_interval`** — Does the paper state that a variable it treats numerically is made of ranked or ordered categories — a rank, a graded classification, an ordinal index, a Likert item entered as a number? Fires on the paper's own description of the variable's categories. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a continuous measurement (money, counts, time) or a variable whose category structure the paper never describes. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`estimated_measure_downstream`** — Does the paper state that a variable entering its substantive analysis is itself an estimate produced by a model, a classifier, a scaling procedure, or a set of factor scores? Fires on the paper's own statement that the variable was estimated or predicted (see REPORT-02, which asks every paper to disclose which of its analysed values a model produced). Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a directly recorded variable, or a simple sum of observed items. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`estimated_confounder`** — Fires when the paper states that a control variable in its analysis is such a model output. Near-miss: a recorded covariate, however imperfect, does not fire it. Unclear: NA.
- **`declared_cutoff`** — Fires when the paper states that it applied a numeric cutoff to build its measure — a threshold for membership, for dichotomising, or for classifying. Near-miss: a conventional significance level, or a cutoff in a robustness appendix that does not produce the analysed measure, does not fire it. Unclear whether a cutoff produced the measure: NA.
- **`reference_text_scaling`** — Does the paper state that the text scale's endpoints or reference points were set by designated anchor, training, or reference documents whose positions the analyst supplied? Fires on the paper naming those anchor documents. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a scaling model the paper describes as estimating positions without supplied anchors. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`cross_unit_latent_comparison`** — Does the paper state that it compares estimated latent scores across groups, periods, chambers, or item sets — for instance saying that units moved, that one group sits higher than another, or that scores from different periods are put on one scale? Fires on that stated comparison of estimated scores. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: reporting scores within a single group and period, or comparing directly observed variables. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`cross_context_measure`** — Does the paper state that one measurement instrument was applied across settings it describes as different — several countries, languages, historical periods, or distinct populations? Fires on the paper's own description of the spread of its cases. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a large sample drawn from one setting, or several settings measured with instruments the paper describes as separate and unconnected. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`administered_instrument`** — Does the paper state that it put questions, items, tasks, or stimuli to respondents or subjects and recorded their answers? Fires on the paper's own description of fielding an instrument (a survey battery, a questionnaire, an experimental task producing a recorded response). Near-miss that does NOT fire it: analysing an existing survey file, administrative records, or text produced for other purposes, without the paper saying it administered anything itself. If it is unclear whether the paper administered its own instrument, the trigger does not fire and every check gated on it is NA; a coder therefore never chooses between NA and FLAG for the same paper.
- **`modified_instrument`** — Does the paper state that it changed an existing instrument — dropping, adding, or rewording items, altering response options, or rescoring it? Does NOT fire: administering a published instrument as originally specified; reporting a published instrument's own alternative short form as published. Unclear whether a change was made: NA.
- **`new_instrument`** — Does the paper state that it created the measure itself — new items, a new coding scheme, a new index built for this study? Near-miss that does NOT fire it: adapting a named existing instrument (that is `established_instrument` plus REPORT-10), or assembling variables that already exist in a dataset. Ambiguity resolves out: NA, not FLAG.
- **`human_coding`** — Does the paper state that people read, watched, or listened to material and assigned codes or categories to it for this study? Fires on the paper's own description of coders, coding, or content analysis. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: survey respondents answering about themselves, experts rating units on a scale (that is `expert_ratings`), or the paper using someone else's already-coded dataset without coding anything itself. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`supervised_classifier`** — Does the paper state that it trained a classifier or learner on cases it labelled by hand and applied it to unlabelled cases? Does NOT fire: a regression predicting a substantive outcome; applying a model built by someone else without stating that this paper trained one (that fires transported_instrument); a dictionary applied without training. Unclear: NA.
- **`expert_or_coder_ratings`** — Fires when the paper states that the values it analyses were assigned by two or more human raters, coders, or experts judging units. Near-miss: a single author coding all cases alone, or survey respondents answering about themselves, does not fire it. Unclear how many people assigned the values: NA.
- **`expert_ratings`** — Does the paper state that its values come from experts, judges, or raters scoring units on a response scale — either ratings it collected or a named expert-survey dataset? Fires on that self-description. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a single author coding cases, or coders applying a categorical codebook to documents (that is `human_coding`). Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`cross_validation_reported`** — Does the paper state that performance was estimated by cross-validation, repeated splitting, or a held-out fold procedure? Fires on that stated procedure. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a single train/test split reported as such (that is covered by IDENT-10), or accuracy reported with no stated estimation procedure. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
- **`case_level_coding`** — Does the paper state that it assigned scores to a set of named cases (countries, parties, episodes, organizations) on the basis of case knowledge, historical or secondary sources? Fires on the paper's own description of case-by-case coding. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: coding a large sample of anonymous documents or respondents (that is `human_coding`), or importing a published country-year index without coding cases itself. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.

## IDENT

*Identification — the assumptions the causal claim rests on.*

### MEASUREMENT-IDENT-01 — A paper must support its main measured variable with more than one kind of evidence that it captures the concept it is named after.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (7 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should back its main measured variable with at least two different kinds of evidence that it captures the concept it is named after, such as comparison with an outside record or a test of a predicted relationship, reported or cited from specific studies.

**Why it matters:** Each kind of evidence covers only part of the case, and no design or sample size can fix a measure that misses its target.

**Check:** How many distinct kinds of evidence the paper reports, or cites a named source as reporting, for the claim that its principal measured variable stands for the concept it is named after.

- **Pass:** For its main measured construct the paper reports at least two distinct kinds from this list, or cites specific studies reporting them: a comparison of the measure against an outside record or criterion variable; a stated check of the instrument's content against the paper's own definition; agreement with a different instrument for the same concept; a test of an association the theory predicts; a fitted measurement model for the item set; human checking of machine-assigned values; re-examination of individual cases' scores against knowledge of those cases. Evidence in an appendix, supplement, footnote, or replication archive counts exactly as main-text evidence does.
- **Flag:** The paper names a construct and analyses values for it while reporting fewer than two of the enumerated kinds anywhere and citing no source that reports them. Reporting none of them, and resting the whole case on a single kind, both take FLAG; the reviewer records which of the two applies.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Robert Adcock, David Collier (2001) Measurement Validity: A Shared Standard for Qualitative and Quantitative Research. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055401003100 — pp. 532, 537
  - Edward G. Carmines, Richard Zeller (1979) Reliability and Validity Assessment. https://doi.org/10.4135/9781412985642
  - Jessica Kay Flake, Eiko I. Fried (2020) Measurement Schmeasurement: Questionable Measurement Practices and How to Avoid Them. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245920952393 — p. 458
  - Jason Seawright, David Collier (2014) Rival Strategies of Validation. Comparative Political Studies. https://doi.org/10.1177/0010414013489098 — p. 132

### MEASUREMENT-IDENT-02 — A paper must not offer reliability or agreement statistics as evidence that its measure captures the intended construct.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (5 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should not offer reliability or agreement figures, such as coder agreement or how well items hang together, as evidence that its measure captures the intended concept.

**Why it matters:** Consistency shows only that a procedure repeats itself; coders who share the same mistake can agree with each other and still be wrong together.

**Check:** Whether the paper's stated support for the claim that its measure captures the construct is a reliability, agreement, or internal-consistency figure.

- **Pass:** No reliability, inter-coder agreement, test-retest, or internal-consistency statistic is offered in the paper as support for the claim that the measure captures its construct. A paper that reports such statistics only as reliability evidence passes.
- **Flag:** The paper's stated ground for the construct claim is such a statistic — for example that the measure is valid because coders agreed, because the items cohere, or because repeated administration gave the same answer.
- **When silent:** PASS

**Further reading**
  - Edward G. Carmines, Richard Zeller (1979) Reliability and Validity Assessment. https://doi.org/10.4135/9781412985642
  - Daniel McNeish (2018) Thanks coefficient alpha, we’ll take it from here.. Psychological Methods. https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000144 — p. 414
  - Kyle L. Marquardt, Daniel Pemstein (2018) IRT Models for Expert-Coded Panel Data. Political Analysis. https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2018.28 — p. 437

### MEASUREMENT-IDENT-03 — A paper validating against an external standard must give evidence about that standard's own measurement quality.

**Scope:** `external_comparison_validation` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper checks its measure against an outside standard, it should say how well that standard is itself measured, for example its reliability, where it comes from and its known errors, or that it is an official record of the event itself.

**Why it matters:** The comparison rests on the standard, so weakness in the standard can undo the case for the measure.

**Check:** Whether the paper says anything about how well the comparison variable it validates against is itself measured.

- **Pass:** The paper states something about the comparison standard's own measurement quality — a reliability figure for it, a statement of its provenance and error properties, or a cited source giving these. An explicit statement that the standard is an administrative record of the event itself also passes.
- **Flag:** The paper names a criterion, record, or alternative instrument and reports the comparison without any statement about how well that comparison variable is measured.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Robert Adcock, David Collier (2001) Measurement Validity: A Shared Standard for Qualitative and Quantitative Research. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055401003100 — p. 543
  - Edward G. Carmines, Richard Zeller (1979) Reliability and Validity Assessment. https://doi.org/10.4135/9781412985642

### MEASUREMENT-IDENT-04 — A paper offering agreement with another instrument as validity evidence must state the conceptual grounds on which agreement was expected.

**Scope:** `external_comparison_validation` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper uses agreement with another measure as support, it should state the conceptual reason it expected the two to agree, or, if it claims to capture something others miss, what difference it expected and why.

**Why it matters:** Without a stated expectation, any correlation could be read as good news, and close agreement counts against a measure said to capture what others miss.

**Check:** Whether the paper states a conceptual reason for expecting the agreement it reports with another instrument.

- **Pass:** Alongside the reported agreement the paper states why, on conceptual grounds, the two instruments should line up — or, where it claims its measure catches something the others miss, states what divergence it expected and why. The statement may sit anywhere in the paper or its materials; the coder judges whether it is there, not when it was written.
- **Flag:** The paper reports a correlation or agreement with another instrument as support for its measure with no stated conceptual expectation, so that any observed correspondence would have been read as favourable.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Robert Adcock, David Collier (2001) Measurement Validity: A Shared Standard for Qualitative and Quantitative Research. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055401003100 — pp. 540-541
  - Jason Seawright, David Collier (2014) Rival Strategies of Validation. Comparative Political Studies. https://doi.org/10.1177/0010414013489098 — p. 123

### MEASUREMENT-IDENT-05 — A paper must not report as a finding the same relationship it assumed in order to validate its measure.

**Scope:** `nomological_validation` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should not present as a finding the same relationship it assumed in order to show its measure works, unless it says plainly that this relationship was assumed and is not offered as a finding.

**Why it matters:** A relationship taken as true to vouch for a measure cannot later be reported as something the measure discovered.

**Check:** Whether the relationship the paper used to vouch for its measure reappears among the paper's own reported findings.

- **Pass:** The relationship invoked to support the measure is not also presented as a result of the paper; or the paper states explicitly that this relationship was assumed for validation and therefore is not offered as a finding.
- **Flag:** The same relationship is used both as the ground for accepting the measure and as a substantive finding, with no statement that the two roles conflict.
- **When silent:** PASS

**Further reading**
  - Robert Adcock, David Collier (2001) Measurement Validity: A Shared Standard for Qualitative and Quantitative Research. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055401003100 — p. 543

### MEASUREMENT-IDENT-06 — A paper measuring a concept with one item must report that item's error or defend the single-item choice.

**Scope:** `single_item_measure` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When one question stands for a concept, the paper should report how much error that question carries, argue why one question is enough, or state the resulting limit on its conclusions.

**Why it matters:** One question can stand for a concept only if the two move together almost exactly; for many-sided topics they do not, and about half of a single item's variation is error even in well-run surveys.

**Check:** Whether the paper says anything about the error carried by the single item it uses for a named concept.

- **Pass:** The paper reports an estimate of the item's reliability or error variance, or argues why one question suffices for this particular concept, or states the resulting limitation on the inferences it draws from that item.
- **Flag:** A single item carries a named concept through the analysis with no reliability estimate, no argument that one question suffices, and no stated limitation.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Stephen Ansolabehere, Jonathan Rodden, James M. Snyder (2008) The Strength of Issues: Using Multiple Measures to Gauge Preference Stability, Ideological Constraint, and Issue Voting. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055408080210 — pp. 220, 229
  - Kenneth A. Bollen (1989) Structural Equations with Latent Variables. Wiley series in probability and statistics. https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118619179 — p. 17

### MEASUREMENT-IDENT-07 — A paper using an automated text measure must report a validation of that measure on its own corpus.

**Scope:** `automated_text_measure` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper measures something from text automatically, it should check that measure on its own documents, for example by hand-checking a sample or comparing with independently coded values, and report what the check found.

**Why it matters:** How a text method performs on one set of documents says nothing about the next, so its record in other studies does not show it works here.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports a validation of its text-derived measure carried out on the corpus it actually analyses.

- **Pass:** The paper reports a validation exercise performed on its own corpus — hand-checking a sample of the machine output, comparison with independently coded values for the same documents, or a stated comparison of the measure against known facts about those documents — and reports what that exercise found. Where the procedure is of a kind governed by IDENT-10, IDENT-11, IDENT-12, or IDENT-13, that more specific check carries the verdict and this one passes, so a single missing validation is recorded once rather than twice.
- **Flag:** A text-derived variable is analysed with no validation on the paper's own corpus and none of IDENT-10 to IDENT-13 applies to the procedure used; or the measure is supported only by citing the method's performance elsewhere.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Justin Grimmer, Brandon Stewart (2013) Text as Data: The Promise and Pitfalls of Automatic Content Analysis Methods for Political Texts. Political Analysis. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mps028 — pp. 268, 271
  - Klaus Krippendorff (2019) Content Analysis: An Introduction to Its Methodology. https://doi.org/10.4135/9781071878781 — p. 43

### MEASUREMENT-IDENT-08 — A paper measuring from text states the interpretive setting in which its texts were read.

**Scope:** `automated_text_measure` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper measures something from text with a computer procedure, it should state the setting in which the texts are read: who produced them, for what audience, and what the language is taken as evidence about.

**Why it matters:** The same passage can support several reasonable readings, so readers need the frame behind the measure.

**Check:** A passage setting out the frame the analysis works in: who produced the texts, for what audience, and what the analyst takes the language to be evidence about.

- **Pass:** The paper states the setting and standpoint from which its texts are read, in the text or in posted documentation.
- **Flag:** The paper reports text-derived values with no passage stating the frame in which the texts were read.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Klaus Krippendorff (2019) Content Analysis: An Introduction to Its Methodology. https://doi.org/10.4135/9781071878781 — pp. 29-30, 39, 42-43

### MEASUREMENT-IDENT-09 — A paper using a trained text classifier must report its agreement with human labels on documents withheld from fitting, broken out by category.

**Scope:** `supervised_text_classifier` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper uses a trained classifier, a model that sorts documents into set categories, it should compare its labels with human labels on documents held out from training, reporting for each category both what share of its documents it found and how often it was right.

**Why it matters:** Scores on training documents overstate accuracy, and an overall figure hides failures, because these two shares can differ.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports the classifier's agreement with human labels on documents held out of fitting, and whether that performance is broken out by category.

- **Pass:** The paper reports a comparison of machine labels against human labels on documents it states were not used in fitting or tuning the model — through a held-out set or a cross-validation procedure — and reports that comparison category by category: a cross-tabulation of human against machine labels, or per-category figures covering both the share of a category's documents the classifier found and the share of its assignments to that category that were right.
- **Flag:** No comparison with human labels is reported; or figures are reported with no statement that they come from documents withheld from fitting, so a reader cannot tell whether the model was scored on its own training data; or only an overall accuracy or agreement figure is reported; or per-category figures are given for only one of the two directions of error. Each of these is a partial satisfaction and takes FLAG; the reviewer records which.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Justin Grimmer, Brandon Stewart (2013) Text as Data: The Promise and Pitfalls of Automatic Content Analysis Methods for Political Texts. Political Analysis. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mps028 — pp. 279-280
  - Dean Knox, Christopher Lucas, Wendy K. Tam Cho (2022) Testing Causal Theories with Learned Proxies. Annual Review of Political Science. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-polisci-051120-111443 — pp. 424, 439

### MEASUREMENT-IDENT-10 — A paper using model-discovered categories must validate them, and anything derived from them, on its own corpus before substantive use.

**Scope:** `unsupervised_text_categories` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper uses categories or topics a model discovered in its texts, it should validate them on its own documents before drawing conclusions, for example by having people judge whether grouped documents belong together, and validate anything built from them too.

**Why it matters:** Discovered categories need not match the concept of interest and partly reflect the model that produced them; success elsewhere does not carry over.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports a validation of its discovered categories, and of any quantity built from them, before drawing substantive conclusions.

- **Pass:** The paper reports at least one validation of the estimated categories performed on its own corpus — human judgement of whether documents within a category belong together and are separable from other categories, hand-coding a sample under the discovered scheme and checking agreement, or lining up movements in a category's measured attention against events known independently — and reports validation for any derived quantity it analyses.
- **Flag:** Estimated categories, or quantities aggregated from them, carry substantive conclusions with no validation reported on this corpus; citing the method's performance in other applications does not substitute.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Justin Grimmer, Brandon Stewart (2013) Text as Data: The Promise and Pitfalls of Automatic Content Analysis Methods for Political Texts. Political Analysis. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mps028 — pp. 281, 283, 286-287

### MEASUREMENT-IDENT-11 — A paper scoring text with a word list must show the list fits this corpus or state it was built for this problem.

**Scope:** `dictionary_measure` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper scores text with a word list (a dictionary of words tied to a concept), it should state that the list was built for this problem or show that a borrowed list works on these documents.

**Why it matters:** Words carry different meanings in different settings, so a list taken from elsewhere can badly mismeasure unless it is shown to transfer.

**Check:** Whether the paper demonstrates that its word list fits the corpus it is applied to, or reports building the list for this problem.

- **Pass:** The paper states that the word list was built for this corpus or research problem, or reports a demonstration that a borrowed list transfers to this domain — for instance checking list-based scores against hand-coded values for documents from this corpus.
- **Flag:** The paper applies a word list taken from another domain or a general-purpose lexicon and reports neither a transfer demonstration nor a validation on its own documents.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Justin Grimmer, Brandon Stewart (2013) Text as Data: The Promise and Pitfalls of Automatic Content Analysis Methods for Political Texts. Political Analysis. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mps028 — pp. 274-275

### MEASUREMENT-IDENT-12 — A paper scaling text must establish that the dimension it recovered is the one it claims to measure.

**Scope:** `text_scaling` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper places texts or speakers on a scale using a model, it should show that the dimension recovered is the one it claims, for example by comparing placements with known positions or examining the words that drive the scale.

**Why it matters:** A scaling model latches onto whatever variation dominates the words, which may be topic, style, or tone rather than the intended dimension.

**Check:** Whether the paper shows that the dimension its scaling model recovered is the dimension it claims to have measured.

- **Pass:** The paper reports evidence about what the recovered dimension is — placements compared with independently known positions for the same actors, separation of groups known beforehand to sit at opposite ends, or examination of the words driving the dimension — and reports what that evidence showed.
- **Flag:** The paper interprets the recovered dimension substantively with no such evidence reported, taking the model's output to be the intended dimension because the model was intended to recover it.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Justin Grimmer, Brandon Stewart (2013) Text as Data: The Promise and Pitfalls of Automatic Content Analysis Methods for Political Texts. Political Analysis. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mps028 — pp. 291, 293-294

### MEASUREMENT-IDENT-13 — A paper fitting a latent-variable measurement model must examine rival specifications and argue substantively for the one it keeps.

**Scope:** `latent_variable_model` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper fits a latent-variable model (one that infers an unobserved concept from several items), it should examine at least one rival setup and give a substantive reason for the one it keeps.

**Why it matters:** Quite different models can fit the data equally well, and assigning an item to the wrong group can create a significant effect from nothing, so fit statistics alone cannot choose.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports considering specifications other than the one it adopts.

- **Pass:** The paper reports fitting or examining at least one rival specification — a different assignment of indicators to factors, a different number of factors, or an alternative structure it names — and gives a substantive reason for the specification it keeps.
- **Flag:** One well-fitting specification is reported with no rival examined and no substantive argument for preferring it to alternatives that would fit comparably.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Kenneth A. Bollen (1989) Structural Equations with Latent Variables. Wiley series in probability and statistics. https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118619179 — pp. 51, 69, 71-72

### MEASUREMENT-IDENT-14 — A paper fitting a measurement model must argue for the direction of the relation between its items and the construct.

**Scope:** `latent_variable_model` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper fits a measurement model, it should state which way influence runs between its items and the concept, whether the concept drives the items or the items shape the concept, and give a reason.

**Why it matters:** Treating every item as driven by the concept is a substantive choice that is often wrong, so it needs an argument.

**Check:** Whether the paper argues for the direction of the relation between its items and the construct.

- **Pass:** The paper states the direction it assumes between items and construct and gives a reason — an argument about what would change if the construct shifted versus if the item shifted, an appeal to temporal order, or a reported empirical test of the direction.
- **Flag:** The paper fits items as indicators of a construct with no statement about why the influence runs that way.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Kenneth A. Bollen (1989) Structural Equations with Latent Variables. Wiley series in probability and statistics. https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118619179 — pp. 65-66

### MEASUREMENT-IDENT-15 — A paper validating a measure by a reproduced relationship must state the theoretical proposition tested and its source.

**Scope:** `nomological_validation` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper supports its measure by showing it relates to another variable as expected, it should state the expected relationship, say where that expectation comes from, and report the result against it.

**Why it matters:** Saying a measure behaves sensibly proves little; this kind of validation works only from a stated theoretical expectation with a named basis, not an ad hoc guess.

**Check:** Whether the paper states the theoretical proposition behind the relationship it treats as a validity test, and where that proposition comes from.

- **Pass:** The paper states the expected relationship before or alongside the test, attributes it to a named theory, prior literature, or an argument it gives, and reports the estimated relationship against that expectation.
- **Flag:** The paper reports that its measure behaves sensibly, correlates as one would expect, or performs as anticipated, without stating which proposition was expected or where the expectation came from.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Edward G. Carmines, Richard Zeller (1979) Reliability and Validity Assessment. https://doi.org/10.4135/9781412985642
  - Robert Adcock, David Collier (2001) Measurement Validity: A Shared Standard for Qualitative and Quantitative Research. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055401003100 — p. 542
  - Jason Seawright, David Collier (2014) Rival Strategies of Validation. Comparative Political Studies. https://doi.org/10.1177/0010414013489098 — p. 116

### MEASUREMENT-IDENT-16 — A paper entering a fitted measure into a substantive analysis must state what else that measure may register besides the target attribute and what it assumes about it.

**Scope:** `fitted_measure_downstream` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper uses a measure built by a fitted model in its main analysis, it should state what else the measure might pick up besides the intended trait, and either argue that this is absent or say how the analysis handles it.

**Why it matters:** The raw inputs behind such a measure carry information beyond the target, so the measure cannot simply be treated as clean.

**Check:** What the paper says its constructed measure may register besides the attribute it names.

- **Pass:** The paper states what its constructed measure may register besides the target attribute and states what it assumes about that — either that the extraneous influence is absent, with a stated reason, or how the analysis handles it.
- **Flag:** The paper enters a fitted measure into its analysis and treats it as standing for the attribute alone, saying nothing about what else the inputs encode.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Dean Knox, Christopher Lucas, Wendy K. Tam Cho (2022) Testing Causal Theories with Learned Proxies. Annual Review of Political Science. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-polisci-051120-111443 — pp. 427, 438

## EST

*Estimation — whether the estimator recovers the target parameter.*

### MEASUREMENT-EST-01 — A paper reporting alpha for coarse ordered-categorical items must compute it in a way suited to that item format, and must state the response format.

**Scope:** `alpha_reported` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper reports Cronbach's alpha (a reliability figure that summarizes how consistently a set of survey items measure the same thing), it should state how many answer options its items have and, when there are seven or fewer, compute alpha in a way suited to ordered categories.

**Why it matters:** The usual alpha assumes continuous answers; with few ordered categories it understates how strongly items relate, so reliability comes out too low.

**Check:** How many response categories the items carry, and whether the paper says its alpha was computed from a matrix appropriate to that format.

- **Pass:** Items carry eight or more response categories and alpha is reported in the ordinary way; OR, at any category count, the paper states that the coefficient was computed from a polychoric or otherwise categorical-appropriate inter-item matrix, or reports the figure under both treatments.
- **Flag:** Items carry four or fewer response categories, including binary items, and alpha is reported from an ordinary product-moment matrix with no categorical-appropriate figure anywhere; OR items carry five to seven categories and neither a categorical-appropriate figure nor a both-ways comparison is reported; OR the paper reports alpha without stating how many response categories its items offer.
- **When silent:** FLAG
- **Threshold:** cutoff 7; provenance: rule of thumb; borderline band: [5, 7]
- **Inside the band:** Inside the band (five to seven response categories) PASS only if a polychoric or otherwise categorical-appropriate coefficient is also reported, or the figure is reported under both treatments; otherwise FLAG, and mark the item as borderline.

**Further reading**
  - Daniel McNeish (2018) Thanks coefficient alpha, we’ll take it from here.. Psychological Methods. https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000144 — p. 416

### MEASUREMENT-EST-02 — A paper must not report alpha as the reliability of a differentially weighted score.

**Scope:** `alpha_reported` · **Severity if flagged:** LOW · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should not report Cronbach's alpha as the reliability of a score in which items carry different weights; it should use a reliability measure built for weighted scores instead.

**Why it matters:** Alpha is designed for scores in which every item counts equally, so it is the wrong figure for a weighted score.

**Check:** Whether the score whose reliability alpha is reported for is described as differentially weighted.

- **Pass:** Alpha is not offered as the reliability of a score the paper describes as differentially weighted; where weights differ, a reliability index built for weighted composites is reported instead.
- **Flag:** The paper describes its analysed score as weighted — factor-score weights, item weights, a differentially weighted composite — and reports alpha as that score's reliability.
- **When silent:** PASS

**Further reading**
  - Daniel McNeish, Melissa Gordon Wolf (2020) Thinking twice about sum scores. Behavior Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-020-01398-0 — p. 2292

### MEASUREMENT-EST-03 — A paper analysing a summed or averaged score must present evidence bearing on the equal-contribution restriction that score imposes.

**Scope:** `sum_or_average_score` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper adds up or averages items into one score, it should present evidence on whether the items relate to the concept about equally, for example from a factor model, and connect that evidence to its use of a total.

**Why it matters:** Adding items is not neutral arithmetic; it assumes each item reflects the concept equally and with equal noise, which needs support like any other assumption.

**Check:** Whether the paper presents evidence bearing on the equal-contribution restriction that its summed or averaged score imposes.

- **Pass:** The paper reports evidence on whether the items relate to the construct comparably — standardized loadings from a fitted factor model, fit of the equal-weighting specification, or a comparison of the total against model-based scores — and relates that evidence to its use of a total.
- **Flag:** Items are summed or averaged into the analysed variable with no reported evidence on whether they relate to the construct comparably.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Daniel McNeish, Melissa Gordon Wolf (2020) Thinking twice about sum scores. Behavior Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-020-01398-0 — pp. 2289, 2291, 2297, 2301

### MEASUREMENT-EST-04 — A paper scoring a borrowed instrument differently from its validation model must give fresh support for the score it analyses.

**Scope:** `established_instrument` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper borrows an existing instrument, it should say whether it scores it the way the validating study did; if not, it should explain why and give fresh support for its own scoring on its own data.

**Why it matters:** Validity evidence belongs to the scoring that was tested, so it does not carry over to a different scoring.

**Check:** Whether the paper says how the instrument it borrowed was scored in the work that validated it, and whether its own scoring matches.

- **Pass:** The paper states that its scoring follows the structure under which the instrument was validated; or, where it departs, gives a reason and reports support for the scoring it actually uses on its own data.
- **Flag:** The paper cites validation of an existing instrument while scoring it differently — a total where the validation fitted a multi-factor or freely weighted model, a subset of items, a collapsed response scale — with no fresh support for the score it analyses.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Daniel McNeish, Melissa Gordon Wolf (2020) Thinking twice about sum scores. Behavior Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-020-01398-0 — p. 2295

### MEASUREMENT-EST-05 — A paper estimating by sampler reports a convergence diagnostic and the criterion it was judged against.

**Scope:** `mcmc_estimated` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper's estimates come from a sampler (a simulation method that builds estimates from many random draws), it should name a convergence check it ran and the value or standard it was judged against.

**Why it matters:** Sampler results are usable only once the sampler has settled on a stable answer, which a convergence check confirms.

**Check:** Whether the paper names a convergence diagnostic it computed and the value or criterion it required, anywhere including its appendices or replication materials.

- **Pass:** The paper names a convergence diagnostic it applied and states the criterion or value obtained.
- **Flag:** The paper reports sampler-based estimates and names no convergence diagnostic, or names one without stating the criterion or value.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Joshua D. Clinton, Simon Jackman, Douglas Rivers (2004) The Statistical Analysis of Roll Call Data. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055404001194 — p. 369
  - Kyle L. Marquardt, Daniel Pemstein (2018) IRT Models for Expert-Coded Panel Data. Political Analysis. https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2018.28 — p. 453

### MEASUREMENT-EST-06 — A paper combining items into one variable must report direct evidence on how many dimensions those items span.

**Scope:** `multi_item_scale` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** HIGH (6 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper combines items into one variable, it should report direct evidence on how many distinct dimensions the items cover, such as a factor analysis; a reliability figure like alpha does not count.

**Why it matters:** If the items span separate dimensions, a single combined score blurs what the variable means.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports direct evidence on the dimensional structure of the items it combines.

- **Pass:** The paper reports evidence bearing on dimensionality for its own item set — a factor or item-response analysis, an eigenvalue or fit comparison across dimension counts, or a reported inter-item correlation structure with a stated conclusion about subscales.
- **Flag:** Items are combined into one analysed variable with no reported evidence on their dimensional structure, or with an internal-consistency coefficient standing in for such evidence.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Daniel McNeish, Melissa Gordon Wolf (2020) Thinking twice about sum scores. Behavior Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-020-01398-0 — pp. 2295, 2297
  - Stephen Ansolabehere, Jonathan Rodden, James M. Snyder (2008) The Strength of Issues: Using Multiple Measures to Gauge Preference Stability, Ideological Constraint, and Issue Voting. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055408080210 — p. 221
  - Daniel McNeish (2018) Thanks coefficient alpha, we’ll take it from here.. Psychological Methods. https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000144 — p. 417

### MEASUREMENT-EST-07 — A paper fitting a category-discovering text model by an iterative routine must report that it used more than one starting configuration or report how the solution varies across runs.

**Scope:** `unsupervised_text` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper finds categories or topics with a model fitted by step-by-step adjustment, it should report using more than one starting point or describe how the categories change across runs.

**Why it matters:** Such routines can settle on different solutions depending on where they start, so one run cannot be presented as the grouping the texts contain.

**Check:** What the paper says about starting values and about variation across runs of the iterative routine that fitted its categories or topics.

- **Pass:** The paper states that it fitted the model from more than one starting configuration, or reports what changes in the recovered categories across runs.
- **Flag:** The paper reports a single fitted solution from an iterative category-discovering routine and says nothing about starting values or run-to-run variation.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Justin Grimmer, Brandon Stewart (2013) Text as Data: The Promise and Pitfalls of Automatic Content Analysis Methods for Political Texts. Political Analysis. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mps028 — pp. 281, 283

### MEASUREMENT-EST-08 — A paper measuring a concept whose parts are all required must score it by a rule that blocks compensation among the parts.

**Scope:** `conjunctive_construct` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper's concept requires every one of its parts, the scoring rule should clearly prevent a case low on any required part from scoring high overall, for example by taking the minimum across parts.

**Why it matters:** Sums and averages let strength on one part make up for weakness on another, which discards the claim that every part is required.

**Check:** Whether the rule that produces the score can award a high value to a case that is low on one of the required parts.

- **Pass:** The score is built by a rule that blocks compensation — the minimum across parts, a required threshold on each part, a product or geometric rule, or another stated rule under which a case in the bottom range of any required part cannot reach the top range of the overall scale. Where the rule as stated does not let a coder settle that question, the check takes FLAG.
- **Flag:** A concept whose parts the paper describes as all required is scored by a sum, an unweighted or weighted mean, or a factor score, so that a case low on one required part can still land high on the scale.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Alexander Wuttke, Christian Schimpf, Harald Schoen (2020) When the Whole Is Greater than the Sum of Its Parts: On the Conceptualization and Measurement of Populist Attitudes and Other Multidimensional Constructs. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055419000807 — pp. 357-358, 361

### MEASUREMENT-EST-09 — A paper building a composite must report the associations among its components.

**Scope:** `multi_item_scale` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper builds a combined index, it should report the correlations among its components.

**Why it matters:** How much each part actually moves the index depends on how it correlates with the others, not only on its nominal weight, so readers need these figures to see what drives it.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports the associations among the components entering its composite.

- **Pass:** The paper reports the correlations or covariances among its components — a matrix, a table, or reported pairwise figures — anywhere in the paper or its materials.
- **Flag:** A composite is built and analysed with no component-by-component association reported, so a reader cannot tell which part is driving it.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Alexander Wuttke, Christian Schimpf, Harald Schoen (2020) When the Whole Is Greater than the Sum of Its Parts: On the Conceptualization and Measurement of Populist Attitudes and Other Multidimensional Constructs. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055419000807 — pp. 363, 365
  - Jason Seawright, David Collier (2014) Rival Strategies of Validation. Comparative Political Studies. https://doi.org/10.1177/0010414013489098 — p. 125

### MEASUREMENT-EST-10 — A paper analysing a composite of required parts must report component-level results alongside the composite ones.

**Scope:** `conjunctive_construct` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper analyzes an index made of required parts, it should report results for every component alongside the index, either the index plotted against each component or each component's relationship estimated on its own.

**Why it matters:** An added-up index fails for cases low on one part and high on the rest, and a result credited to the whole concept may come from one part.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports component-level results alongside the composite ones.

- **Pass:** The paper reports, for every component, either the composite plotted or cross-tabulated against that component to show whether cases score high while lacking a required part, or the external association estimated with that component on its own beside the composite result.
- **Flag:** Only composite-level results are reported, so a reader cannot tell whether one component carries the relationship or whether high-scoring cases lack a required part.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Alexander Wuttke, Christian Schimpf, Harald Schoen (2020) When the Whole Is Greater than the Sum of Its Parts: On the Conceptualization and Measurement of Populist Attitudes and Other Multidimensional Constructs. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055419000807 — pp. 363, 369-370

### MEASUREMENT-EST-11 — A paper standardizing components before aggregation must state what that does to the meaning of its scores, given the comparisons it makes.

**Scope:** `standardized_before_aggregation` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper standardizes components to its sample before combining them, it should state that the scores are relative to the sample and compare only within it, or justify the meaning of the scales when comparing levels across places or periods.

**Why it matters:** Standardizing makes scores relative to the sample, so on their own they cannot support comparisons across places or periods.

**Check:** Whether the paper states what its rescaling does to the meaning of the resulting scores, given the comparisons it goes on to make.

- **Pass:** The paper states that its scores are relative to this sample and confines its claims to within-sample comparisons; or, where it reports absolute levels or comparisons across periods or places, justifies the substantive meaning of the component scales being combined.
- **Flag:** Components are standardized to the sample and the resulting score is then read as an absolute level, or compared across periods, places, or samples, with no statement about what the rescaling did to its meaning.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Alexander Wuttke, Christian Schimpf, Harald Schoen (2020) When the Whole Is Greater than the Sum of Its Parts: On the Conceptualization and Measurement of Populist Attitudes and Other Multidimensional Constructs. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055419000807 — pp. 371-372

### MEASUREMENT-EST-12 — A paper estimating latent scores must state the restrictions that fix the scale's location, spread, and direction.

**Scope:** `latent_variable_model` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (4 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper estimates scores on a latent scale (one inferred rather than observed), it should state the restrictions that fix the scale's zero point, unit, and direction, and read its estimates in those terms.

**Why it matters:** A latent scale has no built-in zero, unit, or direction, so without such restrictions the estimates have no unique solution and cannot be interpreted.

**Check:** Whether the paper states the restrictions that fix the latent scale's location, spread, and direction.

- **Pass:** The paper states the identifying restrictions or normalization it imposed — fixing a loading, fixing the latent variance, anchoring named units, or the priors that supply location and scale — and reads its estimates in those terms.
- **Flag:** Latent estimates are interpreted substantively with no statement of what fixes the scale's zero, unit, or direction.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Joshua D. Clinton, Simon Jackman, Douglas Rivers (2004) The Statistical Analysis of Roll Call Data. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055404001194 — pp. 357-358
  - Kenneth A. Bollen (1989) Structural Equations with Latent Variables. Wiley series in probability and statistics. https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118619179 — p. 18
  - Kyle L. Marquardt, Daniel Pemstein (2018) IRT Models for Expert-Coded Panel Data. Political Analysis. https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2018.28 — p. 443

### MEASUREMENT-EST-13 — A paper must say whether its final measurement model was reached by revision after seeing fit, and what that does to its reported tests.

**Scope:** `latent_variable_model` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should say whether its final measurement model was revised after seeing how well earlier versions fit; if so, it should give substantive reasons and either note that its tests are affected or confirm the model on new data.

**Why it matters:** Revising a model to improve fit makes its reported tests wrong by an unknown amount, and only fresh data can separate real findings from chance.

**Check:** Whether the paper says whether its final specification was arrived at by revising an earlier one in response to fit.

- **Pass:** The paper states whether the reported specification was revised after seeing fit results; where it was, it says so, gives substantive grounds for the revisions, and either notes that the reported test statistics are affected or reports the revised model on independent data.
- **Flag:** The paper presents a final model whose modification indices, dropped paths, added residual covariances, or reassigned items show it was reached by revision, while reporting its test statistics as if the specification had been fixed in advance.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Kenneth A. Bollen (1989) Structural Equations with Latent Variables. Wiley series in probability and statistics. https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118619179 — p. 61

### MEASUREMENT-EST-14 — A paper analysing ranked categories numerically must justify the measurement level it assumes.

**Scope:** `ordinal_as_interval` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper treats ranked categories (such as low, medium, high) as numbers, it should give grounds for their order and for the equal steps it assigns, or also report results treating them only as ranked.

**Why it matters:** Order and equal spacing are claims to be shown, not assumed, before categories are used in arithmetic.

**Check:** Whether the paper justifies handling its ranked categories at the level of measurement its analysis assumes.

- **Pass:** The paper gives a stated ground for the level at which it analyses the variable — a demonstration that the categories are ordered, an estimate of the spacing between thresholds, an argument for the increments it assigns, or a statement that results are reported under an ordinal treatment as well.
- **Flag:** Ranked or graded categories are scored as numbers and entered into arithmetic with no stated ground for the ordering or for the equality of the increments assigned.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Jason Seawright, David Collier (2014) Rival Strategies of Validation. Comparative Political Studies. https://doi.org/10.1177/0010414013489098 — pp. 119, 121-122

## INFER

*Inference — standard errors, tests, and their validity.*

### MEASUREMENT-INFER-01 — A paper entering an estimated measure into a later analysis must report uncertainty that takes in the measurement stage.

**Scope:** `fitted_measure_downstream` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (6 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper uses an estimated measure in a later analysis, its reported uncertainty should include the uncertainty from estimating that measure, for example by fitting both stages together or repeating the analysis across draws of the measure.

**Why it matters:** Treating an estimated measure as if it were observed exactly makes intervals too narrow.

**Check:** What the paper says about where the uncertainty in its reported downstream estimates comes from.

- **Pass:** The paper states that the uncertainty it reports for its downstream estimates takes in uncertainty from the measurement stage — by fitting the measurement and substantive parts together, by repeated draws of the measure with the substantive analysis run inside each, by resampling the material the measurement model was fitted on, or by a stated correction that names the measurement stage.
- **Flag:** The paper enters point values of a fitted measure into a later analysis and reports standard errors, intervals, or posterior summaries computed as though those values had been observed without error.
- **When silent:** FLAG
- **Prevalence:** Knox, Lucas and Cho (2022) state that correction for first-stage uncertainty is almost never attempted in published proxy-based work, and that posterior uncertainty a measurement model does supply is typically left behind.

**Further reading**
  - Dean Knox, Christopher Lucas, Wendy K. Tam Cho (2022) Testing Causal Theories with Learned Proxies. Annual Review of Political Science. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-polisci-051120-111443 — p. 435
  - Joshua D. Clinton, Simon Jackman, Douglas Rivers (2004) The Statistical Analysis of Roll Call Data. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055404001194 — p. 366

### MEASUREMENT-INFER-02 — A paper must not read a null obtained with an estimated measure as evidence against its hypothesis.

**Scope:** `estimated_measure_downstream` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should not treat a null result obtained with an estimated measure as evidence against its hypothesis; when it reports such a null, it should name a weak measure as a possible explanation.

**Why it matters:** A measure that tracks the concept poorly is a second route to finding nothing, on top of ordinary low statistical power.

**Check:** What the paper concludes from a proxy-based result that shows no association.

- **Pass:** The paper does not read a null obtained with an estimated measure as evidence against the hypothesis; where it reports such a null, it names proxy weakness as an alternative explanation.
- **Flag:** The paper states that a hypothesis is disconfirmed, unsupported, or ruled out on the strength of a null obtained with an estimated measure, without naming the measurement route to a false negative.
- **When silent:** PASS

**Further reading**
  - Dean Knox, Christopher Lucas, Wendy K. Tam Cho (2022) Testing Causal Theories with Learned Proxies. Annual Review of Political Science. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-polisci-051120-111443 — p. 431

### MEASUREMENT-INFER-03 — A paper conditioning on an estimated confounder states that residual confounding remains.

**Scope:** `estimated_confounder` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper controls for a confounder (a factor linked to both cause and outcome) using an estimated version of it, it should state that some confounding may remain, or apply a correction based on the estimate's error.

**Why it matters:** The part of the confounder the estimate misses still links the variables, so the control does not remove the confounding.

**Check:** Whether the paper, having entered an estimated or scored variable as a control, states that residual confounding remains, or instead describes its estimate as adjusted, net of, or controlling for that confounder without qualification.

- **Pass:** The paper states that confounding may remain after conditioning on its estimated control, or reports a correction that uses knowledge of the estimate's error.
- **Flag:** The paper enters an estimated confounder as a control and describes the resulting estimate as adjusted for that confounder with no statement that residual confounding remains.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Dean Knox, Christopher Lucas, Wendy K. Tam Cho (2022) Testing Causal Theories with Learned Proxies. Annual Review of Political Science. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-polisci-051120-111443 — pp. 433-435

### MEASUREMENT-INFER-04 — A paper must not defend its estimate as a lower bound on the ground that measurement error only attenuates.

**Scope:** `all` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** HIGH (3 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** The paper should not call its estimate a lower bound because measurement error only shrinks effects, unless it states that its design meets the conditions: independent error unrelated to true values, modest error, a large sample, and a result not selected for significance.

**Why it matters:** Measurement error does not always shrink estimates; the direction can reverse when error is severe or correlated, or when small-sample results were selected for significance.

**Check:** Whether the paper defends its estimate by asserting that measurement error can only have pushed it toward zero.

- **Pass:** The paper does not invoke attenuation as a defence; or, where it does, states the conditions its own design meets — independent error unrelated to the true values, error of modest size, a large sample, and a result not selected for having reached significance.
- **Flag:** The paper argues that its estimate is conservative, a lower bound, or would only be larger with better measures, without stating the conditions under which that direction holds.
- **When silent:** PASS

**Further reading**
  - Eric Loken, Andrew Gelman (2017) Measurement error and the replication crisis. Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aal3618 — pp. 584-585
  - Stephen Ansolabehere, Jonathan Rodden, James M. Snyder (2008) The Strength of Issues: Using Multiple Measures to Gauge Preference Stability, Ideological Constraint, and Issue Voting. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055408080210 — p. 218

## ROBUST

*Robustness — sensitivity, diagnostics, and alternative specifications.*

### MEASUREMENT-ROBUST-01 — A paper building its measure with a numeric cutoff either states a substantive ground for that value or reports its focal quantity at more than one value.

**Scope:** `declared_cutoff` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper builds its measure using a numeric cutoff, it should give a substantive reason for the value chosen or report its main result at more than one cutoff.

**Why it matters:** Obvious cutoffs are often unavailable, so a threshold leaves room for arbitrary or convenient choices.

**Check:** Whether the paper gives a substantive ground for the cutoff value it used, and whether it reports its focal quantity at any second cutoff value, in the text or its supplements.

- **Pass:** The paper states a substantive ground for the cutoff it applied, or reports its focal quantity at two or more distinct cutoff values.
- **Flag:** The paper builds its measure with a cutoff, gives no substantive ground for that value, and reports no result at any other value anywhere.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Alexander Wuttke, Christian Schimpf, Harald Schoen (2020) When the Whole Is Greater than the Sum of Its Parts: On the Conceptualization and Measurement of Populist Attitudes and Other Multidimensional Constructs. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055419000807 — pp. 360, 363

### MEASUREMENT-ROBUST-02 — A paper fitting a covariance-based measurement model must screen for influential cases and report estimates with and without them.

**Scope:** `latent_variable_model` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper fits a measurement model based on covariances (how variables move together), it should screen for unusual cases looking at several variables at once, and report estimates with and without them.

**Why it matters:** A few extreme cases can distort the picture of how variables relate for most of the sample, in either direction.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports screening for influential cases and what their exclusion does to the estimates.

- **Pass:** The paper reports a screen for extreme or influential cases that looks beyond one variable at a time, and reports estimates both with and without the cases it identified.
- **Flag:** A covariance-based measurement model is fitted with no reported screen for influential cases, or with a screen reported but no with-and-without comparison of the estimates.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Kenneth A. Bollen (1989) Structural Equations with Latent Variables. Wiley series in probability and statistics. https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118619179 — pp. 1, 28, 31

### MEASUREMENT-ROBUST-03 — A paper scaling text from anchor documents must identify them and report something bearing on their influence on the estimates.

**Scope:** `reference_text_scaling` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper places texts on a scale using anchor documents (reference texts that define its ends), it should identify them and report something on their influence, such as why they were chosen or results with other anchors.

**Why it matters:** Every estimate depends heavily on the anchors picked, since their style and non-ideological content carry into the scale.

**Check:** Whether the paper identifies the documents it used as anchors and reports anything bearing on how much that choice drives the estimates.

- **Pass:** The paper identifies the documents used as anchors and reports at least one of: the grounds on which they were chosen; estimates under an alternative anchor set; preprocessing undertaken to strip stylistic or technical language; or a comparison of the resulting positions with independently known positions for the same actors.
- **Flag:** Anchor or reference documents are supplied and the resulting positions interpreted while the anchors are not identified, or are identified with nothing reported that bears on their influence.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Justin Grimmer, Brandon Stewart (2013) Text as Data: The Promise and Pitfalls of Automatic Content Analysis Methods for Political Texts. Political Analysis. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mps028 — p. 292

### MEASUREMENT-ROBUST-04 — A paper comparing latent scores estimated from different item sets must state what puts them on a common scale.

**Scope:** `cross_unit_latent_comparison` · **Severity if flagged:** MEDIUM · **Consensus:** LOW (1 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper compares latent scores estimated from different sets of items or periods, it should state what puts them on a common scale, such as shared items or units assumed not to have moved.

**Why it matters:** A shift in the items looks exactly like a shift in the units being measured, so without such a link only relative movement is known.

**Check:** Whether the paper states what puts scores from different item sets or periods onto a common scale.

- **Pass:** The paper states the device that makes the comparison possible — items common to both sets used as bridges, units assumed not to have moved, or another stated normalization — and reads its comparison in those terms.
- **Flag:** Scores estimated from different item sets, periods, or chambers are compared directly, or movement is attributed to units, with no statement of what puts them on a common scale.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Joshua D. Clinton, Simon Jackman, Douglas Rivers (2004) The Statistical Analysis of Roll Call Data. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055404001194 — pp. 362, 364

### MEASUREMENT-ROBUST-05 — A paper applying one measure across settings reports what it did about comparability across them.

**Scope:** `cross_context_measure` · **Severity if flagged:** HIGH · **Consensus:** MEDIUM (2 of the module's sources)

**In plain words:** When the paper applies one measure across settings it describes as different, it should report what it did about whether the measure means the same thing in each, such as testing items across settings or adapting them, and why.

**Why it matters:** The same value can mean different things in different settings, so comparability should be addressed rather than assumed.

**Check:** Whether the paper reports work bearing on whether its measure means the same thing across the settings it covers: a test of item behaviour across settings, a setting-specific adaptation with a stated reason, a stated rescaling, or a stated argument that the same rule applies everywhere.

- **Pass:** The paper reports at least one of those and states the ground for it.
- **Flag:** The paper applies one measure across settings it names as differing and reports nothing bearing on whether its values mean the same thing across them.
- **When silent:** FLAG

**Further reading**
  - Robert Adcock, David Collier (2001) Measurement Validity: A Shared Standard for Qualitative and Quantitative Research. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055401003100 — pp. 534-536, 544
  - Alexander Wuttke, Christian Schimpf, Harald Schoen (2020) When the Whole Is Greater than the Sum of Its Parts: On the Conceptualization and Measurement of Populist Attitudes and Other Multidimensional Constructs. American Political Science Review. https://doi.org/10.1017/s0003055419000807 — pp. 365, 368

## REPORT

*Reporting — what the paper must state for a reader to evaluate it.*
